analysis.one_liner: Bars EPA from regulating coal ash and other coal-burning waste as hazardous waste.
analysis.headline: Despite 65 cosponsors, the bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently change the nation's waste law so that coal ash and other waste from burning coal — fly ash, bottom ash, slag, and smokestack scrubber waste — could never be regulated as hazardous waste. Utilities would keep storing it in ponds and landfills under weaker rules, while roughly 42% of it would continue being recycled into products like concrete and wallboard. The bill was introduced in April 2011, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-burning power plants and coal producers, who would avoid the cost of handling their waste under hazardous-waste rules. Businesses that turn coal ash into concrete, wallboard, and other products would also benefit, because a 'hazardous' label could scare customers away from their product.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal-burning utilities and coal ash recyclers

how_it_helps.text: Exempts fly ash, bottom ash, slag, and flue gas scrubber waste from coal or other fossil fuel combustion from regulation as hazardous waste under the Solid Waste Disposal Act, locking that exemption into law rather than leaving it to EPA's judgment.

The bill's findings note that EPA's own 1993 and 2000 regulatory determinations concluded these wastes did not warrant hazardous-waste regulation, in part because such a label would stigmatize the waste and impede its beneficial reuse.

The findings state that about 42% of these wastes are recycled into concrete, wallboard, bricks, and road materials, and that using coal ash in place of Portland cement in 2007 saved energy equal to the annual use of more than 676,000 households and avoided roughly 12.4 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near coal ash ponds and landfills and drink from groundwater those sites can leak into. Coal ash contains arsenic, mercury, and lead; without the option of hazardous-waste safeguards, contamination would be handled — or not — under weaker non-hazardous rules. Any future taxpayer-funded cleanups of contaminated sites would also be more expensive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near coal ash disposal sites

drawbacks.text: The bill removes EPA's ability to ever apply hazardous-waste rules to coal combustion waste, no matter what future evidence shows about leaks from ash ponds and landfills into groundwater — a risk EPA was actively considering in a proposed rule on coal ash disposal published in June 2010.

Supporters would acknowledge the tradeoff they are accepting: keeping the 'non-hazardous' label protects the recycling market, but it also means storage of the remaining waste in ponds and landfills stays under the lighter-touch rules that have produced well-known ash impoundment failures.

An honest cost of the bill's approach: writing the exemption into statute takes the decision permanently out of regulators' hands, so even a future EPA that found the waste hazardous could not regulate it as such.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine upside is protecting a large recycling market that displaces cement and saves energy, and the EPA determinations it cites did support non-hazardous treatment as of 2000. But the bill goes further than preserving recycling: it permanently strips regulators of the power to treat coal ash as hazardous even if evidence of water contamination accumulates, putting the disposal side of the problem — the ponds and landfills where most ash ends up — beyond the stricter rules. The recycling benefit is real; the permanent legal shield for disposal practices is the costly part.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's environment subcommittee, which held one markup session in June 2011, and then no further action ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative David McKinley of West Virginia introduced the bill on April 6, 2011, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy.

Sixty-five representatives cosponsored the bill — 53 Republicans and 12 Democrats, including several Democrats from coal-producing districts such as Nick Rahall of West Virginia, Tim Holden and Mark Critz of Pennsylvania, and Jason Altmire of Pennsylvania.
The subcommittee held a consideration and markup session on June 16, 2011, but the bill was never reported out of the full committee and never received a vote in either chamber.
The bill died at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013, having never advanced past its subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The coal ash recyclers and coal-burning utilities gained the least from the bill's death, while communities near ash sites and water consumers were spared a permanent statutory bar on hazardous-waste regulation. EPA kept full authority over coal ash, which it later used.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near coal ash sites kept EPA oversight

sides.party_line_note: Of 65 cosponsors, 53 were Republicans and 12 were Democrats, largely from coal-producing states, so the bill had a bipartisan core but leaned heavily Republican; its failure came from inaction rather than an opposing vote.

industries.note: The bill would shield the waste these plants produce — tens of millions of tons of ash, slag, and scrubber sludge a year — from ever being regulated as hazardous, cutting their disposal compliance costs. The cost lands on nearby communities whose groundwater those ponds and landfills can contaminate.

Weaker rules for burning coal's waste lower the effective cost of coal-fired generation, supporting demand for mined coal. The environmental and health risks of ash disposal are externalized to the public.

industries.industry: Coal ash recyclers and concrete and wallboard manufacturers
industries.note: The bill protects their feedstock by making the 'non-hazardous' label permanent, since a hazardous designation could stigmatize ash-based products — the bill text itself argues a label would impede beneficial use. Recycled ash genuinely displaces cement and cuts emissions, but the statute would also lock in the arrangement regardless of future evidence.

State and local authorities would lose the federal backstop of hazardous-waste rules for coal ash, leaving cleanup and oversight of ponds and landfills to weaker state-level non-hazardous regimes — a burden shift that generally works against communities.
